body.heading: Sowing seeds, harvesting strategy
paragraphs: Mancala is not one game but a family of hundreds, all sharing one beautiful move: lift every stone from one of your pits and drop them, one at a time, into the pits that follow — sowing, as farmers sow seed. Captures, stores and winning conditions vary by region, but the rhythm is universal.

In Ghana, oware is a game of national pride and fierce calculation. Congkak is played across Malaysia and Indonesia, traditionally with shells or seeds on a boat-shaped board. Bao, from East Africa, is considered one of the most complex board games in the world — masters study it like chess.

body.heading: Counting that feels like farming
paragraphs: Every mancala move is arithmetic in disguise: you count a pit's stones, forecast where the last stone will land, and plan captures several sowings ahead. Good players “keep the rhythm” of the board the way farmers know their fields — by constant, affectionate attention.

The games also carry a social rule as old as the boards: play is conversation. Matches in markets and courtyards gather spectators, advice and laughter; winning matters, and so does being worth playing against.

body.heading: Try it: an egg-box mancala
paragraphs: An egg carton makes a perfect twelve-pit board, with a small bowl at each end as stores. Put four counters in each pit and play the simplest kalah rules: sow anti-clockwise; if your last stone lands in your store, take another turn; if it lands in an empty pit on your side, capture that stone and the pit opposite.
Play a match of three games and swap strategies afterwards. You will find the second game is nothing like the first — that is five hundred years of players talking.

takeaway: Mancala turns counting into farming and farming into strategy: sow carefully, and the board will feed you.
